problem: Hand-crafted RL rewards and model-based planners like ORCA cannot capture implicit social rules such as yielding and deadlock avoidance in narrow crossings, and existing MEDIRL only handles static scenes and needs many demonstrations.
motivation: Social behaviors (yielding, legibility) are intuitive to humans but hard to specify as rewards or rules. Learning a reward map from few expert demonstrations, conditioned on scene geometry and agent trajectories, could encode these behaviors implicitly without handcrafted features.
key_idea: Extend Maximum Entropy Deep IRL to dynamic scenes by extrapolating few-shot demonstrations with noisy start positions and adding a bilateral-filter smoothing loss on the learned reward, then execute sampled trajectories with an ORCA controller.
insight: Extrapolating demonstrations helps cover unseen states but adds noisy reward aberrations and local minima; the bilateral smoothing loss (emulating a costmap inflation layer) removes them. Success rose from about 82% (MEDIRL) to about 92% (S-MEDIRL), and both IRL agents avoid deadlock without explicit deadlock logic, finishing faster than the rule-based backoff agent (about 30 s faster).
method: MDP formulation: 60x60 top-down grid over 6x6 m centered on the door; actions up/down/left/right/stay; deterministic transitions.

MEDIRL backbone: U-Net predicts a per-pixel reward map from stacked features; the loss gradient is the difference between expert and sampled state visitation (mu_D - E[mu]) plus a regularizer; reference trajectories are 10 steps ahead, sampled every 0.1 s.
Input features: RGB channels of the top-down image, robot past trajectory, human past trajectory, human heading and velocity, and robot goal.

Demonstration extrapolation: 15 demonstrations over 7 start/goal configs are augmented with 6 random start positions near the robot start, plus explicit counter-stop (3 s threshold) points so the robot learns to wait.
Bilateral smoothing loss: spatial-and-range Gaussian weighted squared reward differences over pixel neighborhoods, added to the MEDIRL loss to remove noise-induced local optima.
Online deployment: the reward is inferred and a trajectory sampled and replanned every 0.2 s; an ORCA local controller tracks it.
Baselines: ORCA with a shortest-path reference, and ORCA-Backoff with a rule-based deadlock detector (moves <0.1 m over 50 steps, then retreats to start and waits).

setting.backbone: U-Net reward network (MEDIRL, trained from scratch) + ORCA local controller
setting.training_data: 15 human expert demonstration data points over 7 start/goal configurations in one Habitat-Sim scene, extrapolated with 6 random nearby start positions per trajectory
setting.observation: low-resolution top-down RGB image plus known human/robot positions, human heading and velocity, and known robot goal
setting.action_space: discrete grid moves (up/down/left/right/stay) for the reward planner; ORCA velocities for execution
setting.privileged: known agent positions, human trajectory/velocity/heading, robot goal, and known scene geometry used for demonstration extrapolation

numbers.eval_set_note: 13 unseen episodes, 5 runs each, same scene as training
numbers.extra: few-shot demos with extrapolation and bilateral smoothing loss
numbers.evidence: Fig. success caption: 'our S-MEDIRL is able to successfully navigate the scene 92% of the time'; text: 'bring up the average success rate to about 92%'
'The average success rate for this agent is similar to the Backoff agent, about 82%'

numbers_note: Results are mainly in figures (per-episode success bars, completion times); only approximate average success rates are stated in the text. Baseline values not listed.
results: S-MEDIRL reaches about 92% success on 13 unseen narrow-crossing episodes versus about 82% for plain MEDIRL and a similar rate for ORCA-Backoff; nominal ORCA deadlocks on all but three episodes. IRL agents complete tasks about 30 s faster than ORCA-Backoff on deadlock episodes.
limitations: Single scene, one human, and only 13 test episodes; generalization to other scenes and multiple agents untested.
Relies on good demonstrations and on privileged info (known goal, human state, scene geometry) with no real-robot tests; success metrics are only approximate and results are mostly in figures.
Uses ORCA local controller and coarse discrete grid; goodness of demonstrations is not quantified.
